Combination Sum I (LC39) — unlimited reuse
blocks.py:
def comb(i, rem, c, cur, out):
    if rem == 0: out.append(cur[:]); return
    for j in range(i, len(c)):
        if c[j] > rem: break
        cur.append(c[j])
        comb(j, rem - c[j], c, cur, out)   # SAME j: reuse allowed
        cur.pop()

items.title: Subsets (power set)
items.statement: All subsets of distinct ints; also loop-based doubling variant for contrast.

solutionCode.label: pick / not-pick, plus the bitmask doubling variant
solutionCode.py:
def subsets(a: list) -> list:
    out, cur = [], []

    def rec(i):
        if i == len(a):
            out.append(cur[:])      # leaf: one full decision set (COPY it)
            return
        cur.append(a[i])            # PICK
        rec(i + 1)
        cur.pop()                   # undo -- backtracking is a REVERSIBLE edit
        rec(i + 1)                  # NOT PICK

    rec(0)
    return out


def subsets_mask(a: list) -> list:
    """Bitmask variant: bit j set means a[j] is in the subset."""
    n = len(a)
    return [[a[j] for j in range(n) if mask & (1 << j)]
            for mask in range(1 << n)]

items.complexity: Time O(n * 2^n) — 2^n subsets, each costing O(n) to copy out. Space O(n) recursion depth plus the output.

followups.q: Why copy cur at the leaf instead of appending it directly?
followups.a: cur is one shared buffer that keeps mutating as the recursion continues. Appending it stores a reference, so every stored "subset" ends up pointing at the same list — empty at the end. The copy is what freezes the state at that leaf. This is the single most common backtracking bug.

followups.q: Why must the pop come between the two calls?
followups.a: It restores cur to exactly the state the frame received, so the not-pick branch explores a clean tree. Backtracking is defined by that symmetry: every mutation before a recursive call is undone after it. Skip the pop and the second branch inherits the first branch's choice.

items.title: Print All Subsequences of String

solutionCode.label: same tree, characters instead of ints
solutionCode.py:
def all_subsequences(s: str) -> list:
    """CONVENTION: the empty subsequence IS included, so 2^n results."""
    out, cur = [], []

    def rec(i):
        if i == len(s):
            out.append("".join(cur))
            return
        cur.append(s[i])        # PICK
        rec(i + 1)
        cur.pop()               # undo
        rec(i + 1)              # NOT PICK

    rec(0)
    return out

items.complexity: Time O(n * 2^n), space O(n) recursion depth.

followups.q: Does the empty string count?
followups.a: Under this convention yes — every position choosing "not pick" is a legitimate leaf, giving exactly 2^n results. Some problem statements exclude it and expect 2^n - 1. Ask, or state your convention; silently picking one is how you get a wrong answer on an otherwise correct solution.

followups.q: Subsequence versus substring?
followups.a: A subsequence keeps relative order but allows gaps — "ace" is a subsequence of "abcde". A substring must be contiguous. There are 2^n subsequences but only n(n+1)/2 + 1 substrings, which is why substring problems are usually polynomial and subsequence problems usually are not.

items.title: Subsequence Sum = K exists

solutionCode.label: boolean tree with early exit

items.complexity: Time O(2^n) worst case, but the OR short-circuits so a hit returns immediately. Space O(n) depth.

followups.q: Why check target == 0 before the index guard?
followups.a: So a solution found at the last element is reported without needing another frame, and so the empty subsequence answers target 0 as True. Putting the index check first means reaching i == n with target 0 returns False — wrong on the trivial case.

followups.q: Would this early-exit optimisation work for the counting version?
followups.a: No. R204 must explore every branch to total them, so there is nothing to short-circuit. Existence questions can prune the moment they succeed; counting questions cannot. That distinction decides whether pruning is available at all.

items.title: Count Subsequences Sum K

solutionCode.label: return the SUM of both worlds instead of the OR

items.complexity: Time O(2^n) — every branch must be explored, no pruning possible. Space O(n) depth.

followups.q: Why must the base case reach i == n rather than stopping at target == 0?
followups.a: Stopping early would count one subsequence and then miss all the ways the remaining elements could also sum to zero — with zeros or cancelling negatives in the array, several distinct subsequences share a prefix. Every leaf must be a complete decision over all n elements for the count to be exact.

followups.q: How does this become dynamic programming?
followups.a: The state is (i, target), and the same pair recurs across many branches. Memoising it gives O(n * sum) time — the subset-sum DP. The recursion is already the DP recurrence; adding a cache is the only change.

items.title: Combinations (n choose k)

solutionCode.label: start-from-i kills permutation duplicates; prune when too few remain
solutionCode.py:
def combine(n: int, k: int) -> list:
    out, cur = [], []

    def rec(start):
        if len(cur) == k:
            out.append(cur[:])
            return
        # PRUNE: need this many more, only (n - i + 1) candidates remain
        need = k - len(cur)
        for i in range(start, n - need + 2):
            cur.append(i)
            rec(i + 1)          # i+1: strictly ascending, no reuse
            cur.pop()

    rec(1)
    return out

items.complexity: Time O(k * C(n,k)) — one O(k) copy per emitted combination. Space O(k) depth.

followups.q: Why does start-from-i eliminate duplicates?
followups.a: Combinations are unordered, so [1,2] and [2,1] are the same answer. Forcing each next pick to come after the previous index means every combination is generated in exactly one order — ascending — so it can only be produced once. Without it you generate permutations and then have to dedupe.

followups.q: State the prune bound.
followups.a: If you still need `need` more elements, the loop cannot start later than n - need + 1, because there would be too few candidates left to ever reach length k. Without it the recursion descends into branches that provably cannot succeed — correct but wasteful, and it is the difference between C(n,k) and considerably more work.

items.title: Combination Sum I
items.statement: Section code; trace your own example aloud.

solutionCode.label: recurse with the SAME index to allow reuse

items.complexity: Time O(n^(target/min)) in the worst case — bounded by how deep the reuse can go. Space O(target/min) depth.

followups.q: Where exactly is the reuse encoded?
followups.a: In the recursive call passing `i` instead of `i + 1`. That single character is the difference between Combination Sum I (unlimited reuse) and Combination Sum II (each element once). Everything else about the two solutions is identical.

followups.q: Why does the recursion terminate despite reusing the same index?
followups.a: Because target strictly decreases on every pick, and all candidates are positive. The depth is bounded by target divided by the smallest candidate. If zero or negative values were allowed, the reuse branch would never terminate — which is why the problem guarantees positives.

items.title: Letter Combinations of Phone Number

solutionCode.label: one loop level per digit

items.complexity: Time O(4^n * n) — up to 4 letters per digit, n digits, O(n) to build each string. Space O(n) depth.

followups.q: Why does empty input return an empty list rather than [""]?
followups.a: The base case would naturally emit the empty string — one combination of zero letters. But the problem specifies no combinations for no digits, so the guard is required. It is a stated convention, not a derivable one, which is exactly why it needs an explicit branch.

followups.q: Why 4^n and not 3^n?
followups.a: Digits 7 and 9 map to four letters each; the rest map to three. The worst case is an input of all 7s and 9s, giving 4^n. Quoting 3^n understates it by a factor of (4/3)^n — at n = 10 that is nearly 18x.

items.title: Generate Parentheses

solutionCode.label: prune by validity: never close more than you opened
solutionCode.py:
def generate_parenthesis(n: int) -> list:
    out, cur = [], []

    def rec(open_count, close_count):
        if len(cur) == 2 * n:
            out.append("".join(cur))
            return
        if open_count < n:              # room for another '('
            cur.append("(")
            rec(open_count + 1, close_count)
            cur.pop()
        if close_count < open_count:    # only close what is already open
            cur.append(")")
            rec(open_count, close_count + 1)
            cur.pop()

    rec(0, 0)
    return out

items.complexity: Time O(4^n / sqrt(n)) — the nth Catalan number of valid strings. Space O(n) depth.

followups.q: Why prune during construction rather than generating and filtering?
followups.a: Generating all 2^(2n) strings and validating each is astronomically wasteful — for n=10 that is a million strings to find 16796 valid ones. The two conditions guarantee every prefix is already valid, so the tree only ever visits nodes that can lead to an answer. No leaf is ever discarded.

followups.q: Why is `close < open` the right condition, not `close < n`?
followups.a: It enforces the prefix invariant: at every point, closes must not exceed opens, or the string is already invalid. `close < n` would allow ")(" — correct counts, invalid nesting. The condition encodes the structural rule, not just the arithmetic one.

items.title: Letter Case Permutation
items.statement: Letters branch two ways; digits pass through.

solutionCode.label: branch only at letters; digits pass straight through

items.complexity: Time O(2^L * n) where L is the number of letters. Space O(n) depth.

followups.q: Why is the result count 2^L and not 2^n?
followups.a: Only letters branch. A digit contributes exactly one child, so it multiplies the count by 1. For "a1b2" there are two letters, giving 4 results — not 16. Quoting 2^n overstates the work whenever the input is digit-heavy.

followups.q: Why restore the character before returning?
followups.a: The buffer is shared across the whole recursion. Leaving it uppercase means the caller's frame — and every sibling branch above it — sees a mutated string. Restoring keeps the invariant that a frame returns the buffer exactly as it found it, which is what makes backtracking composable.

items.title: Target existence with THREE ops (+,-,concat digits)
items.statement: Given digit array & target T: does some ± assignment hit T?
hints: Two-way branch per element with signed adds.
Generalizes directly to LC494 next level.

solutionCode.label: two-way signed branch per element

items.complexity: Time O(2^n) — two signs per element. Space O(n) depth. Memoising on (i, running) makes it O(n * range), which is LeetCode 494.

followups.q: How does this differ from the subsequence-sum tree?
followups.a: There, "not pick" contributed nothing. Here every element must be signed, so both branches contribute — plus or minus, never absent. That is why the base case tests the full running sum rather than a remaining target, and why the tree has no leaves that skip elements.

followups.q: How does it become LeetCode 494?
followups.a: Change the OR to a PLUS and the boolean base to 1 or 0 — that is Target Sum exactly. Memoising on (i, running) turns 2^n into O(n * S) where S is the sum range, and the classic reduction rewrites it as a subset-sum counting DP over (S + target) / 2.
